title: ‘Mercigiving’ Is More Than Just a Parisian Dinner Party
summary:
Now that I live in Paris, it's my turn to host this French Thanksgiving tradition.

The post ‘Mercigiving’ Is More Than Just a Parisian Dinner Party appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Beaujolais Nouveau Day—the date when the year’s vintage can legally be sold, as determined by the French government in 1985—is always on the third Thursday of November. And the fourth Thursday is always Thanksgiving. This, to me, feels preordained by a higher power (God? Mitterand?) because Gamay pairs beautifully with turkey. It’s why, this year, I’ve told my friends to bring a bottle of the young wine to dinner at my new apartment, a top-floor studio under a zinc roof in romantic Montmartre, for Mercigiving.

This is what I call Thanksgiving celebrated in France, which I have done for the past two years. In 2024, I was invited by a friend to a candle-lit soirée at Airelles Le Grand Contrôle, a five-star hotel on the grounds of Versailles, where la grande dinde was presented on a silver platter by a costumed server in a powdered wig. In 2025, I went to a potluck dinner in Paris at the home of another friend where the menu included French onion soup casserole; having passed through the Rhône a few days earlier, I brought a case of fresh Bojo.

During both Thanksgivings, I was still a Brooklynite traveling solo, taking advantage of three PTO days and the long weekend. My gracious hosts introduced me to French citizens and English-speaking Parisians, all stylish, intelligent, and welcoming. A few even wrote letters in support of my application for a French visa—it was time to give it a shot, I’d decided, after my 12th visit to the country and 12 years in New York City. This past May, I arrived in Paris with six suitcases in tow and embraced my pre-made group of friends raising their glasses to my new chapter. 

Loneliness, usually inextricable from the experience of building a life in a new country, has yet to claim me. I realize I am fortunate and that this is not the case for most. One’s duty when one enjoys community is to extend it to others, to pull up a chair for the strangers who need it. For the last two years, I certainly did. Now that I live in Paris, it’s my turn to host Mercigiving.

Yes, it’s tricky shopping at Franprix for whole turkeys or Campbell’s Condensed Cream of Mushroom Soup. I was asked to mule cans of the stuff from the United States last Thanksgiving. But it’s a ritual that, over time, expats and immigrants have successfully folded into the Parisian cultural calendar. The French, even if they don’t get Thanksgiving off, can now do their Christmas shopping during Black Friday sales (occasionally extended and awkwardly renamed to “Black Week”). And, even if eating dinner at 4 pm is anathema to their nature, they’ve developed an appreciation for the holiday meal itself, thanks to restaurants and hotels getting in on the action. 

In Paris, limited-time prix-fixes featuring cranberry sauce and pecan pie during Thanksgiving week are becoming more common. Restaurants like Chocho, Treize au Jardin, and Milagro—all helmed by Franco-Americans—are known for their annual turkey dinners, while hotels like Fouquet’s Paris, La Fantaisie, and the Paris Marriott Champs-Élysées are increasingly targeting Yanks making good use of their limited vacation days.

The palatial Hôtel de Crillon, A Rosewood Hotel, will serve its first-ever Thanksgiving dinner at La Cave, its private dining room-slash-wine cellar. (Tickets to the 12-person table cost 375 euros each—plus 190 euros for the wine pairing.) The Crillon’s executive chef Alan Taudon says he and the hotel are hosting the evening because, “Thanksgiving is a celebration of gratitude, generosity, and togetherness.” It’s as good a reason as any, I agree, to throw a dozen strangers into a room filled with magnums and jeroboams.  

For Carrie Solomon, the chef-owner of Chez Carrie, a “Méditerranéen Californien” bistro that opened last autumn in the second arrondissement, the holiday is also about conjuring a sense of festive community. Solomon has hosted Thanksgiving meals for over 10 years in France, she tells me, and now serves plates of confit turkey at her restaurant over the weekend.

During the three-day service, she welcomes Americans in search of familiar flavors, French folks who simply love a good meal, and friends both old and new. “I love meeting people and bringing everyone together for a harvest celebration,” she says of her Thanksgiving intentions, “being grateful for the end of one season and the beginning of the next.”

Much like Columbus Day, Thanksgiving is a fraught holiday on the American calendar, with its colonial and propagandist roots. Moreover, for many in the U.S., it can feel like a chore or an emotional burden, returning to hometowns and families of origin that may be unwelcoming to them. It’s why Friendsgiving celebrations have become more commonplace—we choose the people with whom we want to spend time, feast, and toast. This persistence and repurposing of Thanksgiving, I believe, means there’s something at its core worth treasuring. 

Like Solomon, I see it as a chance to make time for those I love and take stock of how the year has gone. And like Taudon, I think the holiday is perfect for throwing a fabulous dinner party with plenty of good wine. For me to do this in my adopted home of France—newly arrived in a land that is not my own, with bounty to share and an eagerness to forge friendships—feels a lot like what Thanksgiving is actually meant to be. 

Plus, I appreciate the added layer of meaning in the portmanteau “Mercigiving.” Merci means thanks in French, of course, but there’s some poignance to the idea of giving mercy, sharing compassion. It’s what I found at my very first Mercigiving dinners as a visitor from New York: Hosts and fellow guests quickly made me part of their anglophones-in-Paris family. I basked in that warmth on those chilly nights, glimpsing what my own future dining tables in this city could look like. 

So this year, in addition to asking my guests to bring a bottle of Beaujolais Nouveau to Mercigiving, I’ll encourage them to invite a friend, whether someone new in town or just passing through, who would appreciate the good company—and bring another bottle of wine to share with a community they, as I did, can come to claim as their own.

title: Lifetime Achievement Award Winner Jerry Lohr’s Work Is Far from Over
summary:
A visionary who supported education, elevated sustainability, and put Paso Robles on the global wine map, Jerry Lohr still has big plans for the future.

The post Lifetime Achievement Award Winner Jerry Lohr’s Work Is Far from Over appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Jerry Lohr is celebrating his 90th birthday on January 1, and his work remains far from over. A respectful visionary who supported education, elevated sustainability, and, most of all, put Paso Robles on the global wine map, Jerry Lohr is receiving this year’s Wine Star Award for Lifetime Achievement. 

This honor comes exactly 10 years after he was toasted as an American Wine Legend at the annual Wine Star Awards ceremony. Six years earlier, the American Winery of the Year award went to J. Lohr Vineyards & Wines, the company he started in 1972 by planting some of the first vines in the Arroyo Seco region of Monterey County. By expanding into Paso Robles in the mid-1980s and opening three separate wineries, he built J. Lohr into a Central Coast juggernaut, producing nearly two million cases annually at its peak and managing about 4,000 acres of estate vineyards today.    

“We emphasize quality and value,” Lohr said of how he achieved his goal of developing a business to pass on to his children and theirs. “I am ecstatic now that my children each own more of the company than me! There will be generations to follow.”

He learned about multi-generational companies firsthand growing up as the son of farmers in South Dakota, where his Catholic upbringing introduced him to wine. As Midwestern family-farming traditions began to crumble under the industrial consolidation that came after World War II, Lohr chose to study engineering at South Dakota State. 

But when it was time to decide where to go to grad school, he chose Stanford University, primarily because it was in California, home of the country’s most promising wine industry. “This was always very much in the back of my mind,” said Lohr.

After working for NASA and starting a construction business that helped develop much of what’s become Silicon Valley, Lohr diversified into wine at a time when the Central Coast was still largely untested and considered risky, mainly because it wasn’t the Napa Valley. 

When asked whether he was surprised at how successful the region became, Lohr exclaimed, “I never considered that it wouldn’t be! Now Paso Robles sells more wine than some of the most famous regions of California. That’s hard for people to believe.”

Lohr’s love for the land is rooted in his South Dakota upbringing, and translated immediately to caring for his vines. J. Lohr was one of the first vineyards to receive the Certified California Sustainable Winegrowing distinction from the California Sustainable Winegrowing Alliance. Two of their wines were the first to obtain that CCS seal, and now 30 of their bottlings have earned it.  

But it’s his work on water that keeps Lohr busy these days. His vineyard and cellar innovations have cut the water needed to make a bottle of wine by nearly 40%. 

In addition to philanthropic support of breast cancer research and treatments—to honor his late wife, Carol, who died in 2008—Lohr’s contributions to higher education include support for the Jerome J. Lohr College of Engineering at South Dakota State University; the UC Davis J. Lohr Vineyards & Wines Fermentation Room; and the Justin and J. Lohr Center for Wine & Viticulture at Cal Poly-San Luis Obispo. 

He’s most proud that each of these initiatives is functional over fancy. “Rather than having grand things, we have very practical things,” he said.

A no-nonsense man, Lohr doesn’t mince words when it comes to the precarious state of the wine industry today. “Now is the most fearful I’ve been in all of the years I’ve been in business,” he said. 

But he remains optimistic that people will come back to wine, though he realizes it may never be as big an industry as it once was. “Some professions are in and then out, but wine goes back 2,000 years to biblical times, and even before that,” said Lohr. “There just aren’t that many products that have such a long lifetime.”

title: 8 Blue Cocktail Recipes for No Particular Reason
summary:
From Blue Lagoons to curaçao-spiked margaritas, these blue drinks are delicious any time of year, but especially now.

The post 8 Blue Cocktail Recipes for No Particular Reason appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
The results are in, and the 2026 midterm elections delivered a blue wave—nay, tsunami, with Democrats taking control of both the House and Senate. But beyond the wins and losses, there’s something bigger worth toasting: democracy in action. Americans headed to the polls, made their voices heard, and helped shape the direction of the country. And after months of campaigning, political ads, and nonstop election coverage, we’d say that calls for a drink.

Of course, blue cocktails aren’t exactly an everyday order. Their vibrant hues often come courtesy of blue curaçao, a citrusy orange liqueur, but can also be from other ingredients like Spirulina or even Gatorade (yes, really). From tropical, rum-based concoctions to refreshing gin cocktails, here are some blue drinks worth raising a glass to.

The Blue Hawaii Cocktail

One of the OG blue cocktails, the Blue Hawaii was created in Waikiki in 1957 and combines vodka, spiced rum, pineapple juice, and a squeeze of lemon. Blue curaçao gives the drink its signature ocean-blue hue while adding a hint of orange flavor that complements the sweet pineapple and warm spice of the rum.

The Blue Lagoon Cocktail

Another one of the most recognizable blue cocktails, the Blue Lagoon reportedly dates back to the 1960s, when it was created at Harry’s New York Bar in Paris. Made with vodka, lemonade, and blue curaçao, this refreshing cocktail gets its electric-blue color from the orange-flavored liqueur, which also adds a citrusy sweetness to balance the tart lemonade.

Blue Margarita

A colorful twist on the classic Margarita, the Blue Margarita swaps traditional orange liqueur for blue curaçao, giving it a vibrant blue hue without drastically changing the flavor profile. Made with blanco tequila, fresh lime juice, and blue curaçao, it’s still the same tart, citrus-forward cocktail you know and love, just with a more playful presentation.

The Water Hazard Cocktail

A viral favorite on golf courses, the Water Hazard combines vodka, lemonade, Sprite, and blue Gatorade, which gives the drink its electric blue hue and a hearty dose of hydration. Sweet and slightly tart, it tastes primarily of blue raspberry, with a citrusy kick and a little fizz from the soda.

The Jack Frost Cocktail

Typically associated with the holiday season (but now, voting season), the Jack Frost cocktail is a frosty, tropical concoction that combines white rum, pineapple juice, coconut water, lime juice, and orange liqueurs. Blended with ice for a slushy consistency, it gets its icy blue color from blue curaçao, while Grand Marnier adds a richer citrus flavor that balances the sweetness.

Negroni Azzuro

A colorful riff on the classic Negroni, Dante’s Negroni Azzurro takes inspiration from the Angelo Azzurro (“blue angel”), a blue cocktail popular in Italian nightclubs in the 1990s. Made with gin, dry vermouth, Lillet Blanc, and Luxardo Bitter Bianco, it gets its electric-blue color from a splash of blue curaçao. The result is a spirit-forward, bittersweet cocktail with citrusy notes and a slightly lighter profile than the traditional Negroni.

From the Deep Cocktail

Created for New Orleans tiki bar Latitude 29’s annual Halloween-themed “Spookilau” event, the Terror From the Deep is a tropical rum cocktail with a slightly spooky twist. Aged rum, spiced apple syrup, lemon juice, and macadamia liqueur create a sweet-tart, nutty flavor profile, while blue curaçao gives the drink its ocean-like appearance. For extra fun, garnish with gummy sharks or a miniature treasure chest. (In this case, maybe an American flag.)

Blue Dream Mimosa

Who says mimosas have to be orange? Created at San Diego’s Madison on Park, this big-batch brunch cocktail combines sparkling wine, lemonade, and fresh ginger for a bubbly, citrus-forward drink with a little spice. The Blue Dream Mimosa’s striking blue-green color comes from Blue Majik, a blue spirulina extract that adds a slightly earthy, seaweed-like note, balanced by the tart lemonade. Plus, the recipe makes 10 servings, making it ideal for a celebratory brunch.

title: For a Wine Trip Like No Other, Head to This Breathtaking Chinese Region
summary:
For those curious about viticulture in China, a renovated hotel—now focused on wine—makes Yunnan more accessible than ever.

The post For a Wine Trip Like No Other, Head to This Breathtaking Chinese Region appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
“Try to tell which one is from Bordeaux,” says sommelier Skye Chen as she gestures to the five glasses of red wine in front of me. I’m staying at the first hotel dedicated to wine in Yunnan, China, Songtsam Lodge Cizhong, where Chen works on behalf of wine hospitality consultancy Top|Somm Studio.

From the first sip, I know it’s a fruitless exercise. They all taste fresh yet full-bodied, and my admittedly amateur palate can’t detect the common missteps of New World Bordeaux-style wines like heavy tannins and overly sweet, jammy notes. I hesitate, then point to my favorite, a bold Cabernet Sauvignon with punchy hints of tart blackcurrant and citrus. Chen reveals the bottle with a teasing smile: Château Roduit 2018, made in Badong, a village less than five miles away.

I shouldn’t be surprised. An increasing number of wineries like Château Roduit are producing vintages at extreme elevations of 5,900 to 9,000 feet in the remote Himalayan foothills of northwest Yunnan. Though the region’s wine scene only started to take shape in the last decade, its history of viniculture runs deep, stretching back to the 1880s when French missionaries imported vines to make wine for Catholic mass. Today, a new wave of winemakers from around the world is working alongside Tibetan farming communities who have tended these terraced plots for generations in the fertile Lancang River Valley.

“We are seeing more grape varieties, more distinct regional expressions, and more producers finding different ways to understand and work with their own land,” says Yang Lu, China’s first Master Sommelier and founder of Top|Somm Studio. Though Yunnan is traditionally dominated by Cabernet Sauvignon,  farmers are now experimenting with Syrah, Chardonnay, and Marselan, a crossbreed of Cabernet Sauvignon and Grenache that thrives at high altitudes with minimal intervention.

A little investor star power hasn’t hurt either. In 2016, Ao Yun—which is owned by LVMH and sits under the luxury conglomerate’s Moët Hennessy division, alongside big-name brands like Dom Pérignon and Ruinart—released its first vintage: a Bordeaux-style blend with plum, clove, and honey notes. “It really put Yunnan on the map,” says Janet Z. Wang, a Chinese wine specialist and author of The Chinese Wine Renaissance. Like many of the area’s top wines, Ao Yun’s vintage grows in the shadow of Meili Snow Mountain, a sacred, unclimbed peak in Yunnan’s Diqing Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, where intense sunlight, cool nights, and mineral-rich soils create ideal conditions for winemaking.

A Different Kind of Wine Country

But for many travelers, the wine itself is only half the draw. Because Yunnan sits at the gateway to Tibet, its wineries have become a de facto medium for preserving the region’s traditions. In addition to tastings and pairings, visitors can listen to lamas chant prayers over vines in hopes of a fruitful harvest, learn how to bake cookies with grape must (a local speciality), and even try their hand at pruning vines and picking grapes with farmers. For Songtsam founder and Yunnan native Baima Duoji, keeping that heritage alive was a major incentive to renovate Songtsam Lodge Cizhong and reopen it in 2025 with its own vineyard and winery.

“[At Songtsam] we have always believed that travel should create a deeper relationship between guests and the communities they visit,” says Duoji. “In Cizhong, wine provides a wonderful way to do that because it connects the landscape, agriculture, food, and culture.”

During my stay at Songtsam Lodge Cizhong, I stroll down to the village to see the historic Cizhong Catholic Church, with its ceiling brightly painted in lotuses and yin-yang symbols. The building is surrounded by a century-old vineyard of rose honey grapes planted by French priests. The fruits here are among the only ones of their kind left in the world after the original varietal was eradicated by a pathogen in France. 

A smiling farmer, speaking only in the local language, shows me how he uses crushed walnuts as fertilizer and tenderly hand-picks the grapes. With no grand estates to tour, Yunnan offers a different kind of wine-focused trip rooted in agriculture and community rather than a conventional itinerary packed with posh tasting rooms. As Wang, the wine specialist, puts it, “The experience is intimate, genuine, and modeled on local farming life.”

Wine also serves as a motivator for travelers to look beyond Yunnan’s more familiar routes. “Our hope is that wine tourism will encourage people to stay longer and discover the many layers of Yunnan beyond its better-known destinations,” says Duoji, referring to the historic monasteries and natural marvels, like the scenic canyon named Tiger Leaping Gorge, that draw visitors to the region.

Between tastings, I explore the surrounding mountains, where a mix of Tibetan, Han, Bai, and Naxi traditions shapes daily life. I drive to the Great Bend of the Yangtze River, a dramatic loop of turquoise water not unlike Arizona’s Horseshoe Bend, and hike through forests in search of elusive snub-nosed monkeys—dead ringers for cuddly Star Wars aliens. In a Naxi village in nearby Tacheng, I learn to make tofu by hand, then sit down to a meal of butter tea, yak fried rice, sauteed foraged mushrooms, and rice cakes with fermented bean dip. Of all the wine trips I’ve taken, none have kept me as entertained between tastings, perhaps because this feels like such a departure from the Western wine country script I’ve grown accustomed to: I trade bike rides for Himalayan treks and charcuterie picnics for al fresco hot pot. (It also doesn’t hurt that this is the first wine tour I’ve been on that involves monkeys.)

While it’s easier than ever for travelers to explore Yunnan thanks to a growing slate of dedicated travel companies and hotels in the region, many of its small-batch wineries still require an appointment arranged through a tour operator, says Wang. She recommends working with WildChina, which specializes in custom private trips. Songtsam also offers bespoke tours using its boutique, Tibetan-style properties as home bases. Some of Wang’s favorite wineries include Zaxee, an hour north of Shangri-La; Bao Zhuang, which aims to rival Ao Yun in quality and price; and Xiaoling, known for its single-village terroir series. “It’s great for the purist,” she says.

That sense of place and hyper-locality is Yunnan’s great appeal, says Chen of Top|Somm Studio. “You are not drinking a Yunnan wine somewhere on the other side of the world,” says Chen. “You are right here, surrounded by the mountains, villages, vineyards, and the people who live here.” 

Later, I fly out of Shangri-La with two bottles of Songtsam’s own Chardonnay wrapped in a sweater in my suitcase. I already know the wine won’t taste the same back home in New York City, where I’m not next to snow-capped peaks and strings of fluttering prayer flags. But I’m hoping a sip will put me right back on that mountainside, if even for a moment.

Getting There: The best way to explore Yunnan is with a tour operator such as Songtsam or WildChina, which can arrange accommodations, ground transportation, local activities, and an English-speaking guide. Most trips begin in Shangri-La, the largest city in Diqing Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, which travelers can reach by plane via Kunming, Yunnan’s capital and main transit hub.

title: China Is Finally Falling in Love with Its Own Wines
summary:
After decades of imported wines ruling the marketplace, China's wine drinkers are discovering the wonders of homegrown reds, whites, and sparklers.

The post China Is Finally Falling in Love with Its Own Wines appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
In March 2026, alongside some of the world’s most respected Masters of Wine, sommeliers, and wine writers, I tasted through hundreds of Chinese wines, from spicy Marselan and rich Cabernet Gernischt to pithy Petit Manseng and intensely sweet Vidal. 

My experience as a judge at the Wynn Signature Chinese Wine Awards in Macau, China, was a special one, not just because of the opportunity to taste so many Chinese wines within the country’s borders. At the ticketed seminars, I was surrounded by enthusiastic, wine-loving members of the public—a seemingly even mix of men and women, many of them young—who paid good money to learn about their nation’s wines. They were engaged at levels I’d rarely seen from Western audiences. 

This “new wave” of Chinese wine drinker bucks the stereotype of wine being the domain of wealthy businessmen, seeking only the flashiest, priciest European and Australian reds. While there is truth in this—these kinds of wines did flood the Chinese market in the late 20th and early 21st century—the trope feels tired now. China has come a long way in a very short time. 

Today, it boasts approximately 1,000 wineries and production facilities, with more than 225,000 acres of vines planted across 12 vastly different wine regions, from mountain to desert and everything in between. Growing conditions can be downright brutal—the vast majority of vineyards must be buried to survive cold, snowy winters—and fine winemaking is, with a few exceptions, still finding its feet. 

That said, China has demonstrated that it is quick to learn. The combination of skilled, well-traveled wine professionals and state-of-the-art viticulture and winemaking equipment mean that it’s only a matter of time before Chinese wines rival the world’s best. And, at long last, Chinese consumers are thirsty for all their country has to offer.

In this episode, I sat down with two leading authorities on Chinese wine: Janet Wang and Eddie McDougall.

Janet is a wine writer and the author of the award-winning book, The Chinese Wine Renaissance. She’s a frequent guest on British television, an international wine judge, and writer of a monthly Chinese wine column for China Report.

Eddie is an award-winning fine winemaker—the Proprietor and Oenologist at Australian wine labels E.J. McDougall and The Flying Winemaker. He is also the founder and chairman of the Wynn Signature Chinese Wine Awards, which has rapidly set a globally recognized benchmark for Chinese wine quality.

In this episode, Janet, Eddie, and I talk about the where, what, and how of Chinese wines. We peek behind the curtain at the fascinating technique of burying vines in winter, the cultural barriers that the Chinese historically faced when it came to wine-drinking, why that’s changing, and whether we may see more Chinese wine on our shop shelves and wine lists in future. Tune in!

On Why, Historically, the Chinese Haven’t Embraced Their Own Wines

Janet Wang: “… Chinese people tend to drink wine in a social context. We don’t tend to drink at home by ourselves, right? So wine, for the last 30 years or so, was really attached to this idea of social status. You know, a lot of the wine was given as a gift or being seen to be consumed in a posh restaurant, you know, the sort of setting where you want to show that you’re sophisticated. And really, if that’s your reason to drink wine, then quite frankly, typically people would seek out Bordeaux or Burgundy or these Old World, already very famous wines that would immediately impart this level of sophistication and, you know, that sort of thing. So Chinese people… they’d tend to want to drink Bordeaux, Burgundies. And Bordeaux has this very handy classification system… So Chinese wine by itself didn’t quite carry that sort of cachet.

One thing we skipped was, when reform and opening up started, when China started to make European style wine… there was something called ‘half juice wine.’ …So what that means was grape wine could have been made with the addition of water or fruit juice to make it sweet, diluted, you know, and that practice was allowed up to 2004. After China joined the WTO in 2001, they decided we need to bring our standard to an international sort of level, so that exported wine is what people in the global market would expect. So unfortunately there were also a lot of people, if you tried Chinese wine in the ‘80s, ‘ 90s, up to, you know, 2004, you probably had something not terribly pleasant, certainly not very well made.

So that’s another reason why people may have had a preconceived notion that Chinese wine just wasn’t very good at all. So for those two reasons, Chinese people tended to feel that wine, good wine, top quality wine, was a foreign product. It had to come from France, Italy. Australia, even, you know. Imported wine was considered higher quality than domestically produced wine. And that’s also one of the reasons why it had been quite tricky, even outside of China, to get the Chinese diaspora to really be proud of what China was producing. Most people don’t even know that China was producing wine. And secondly, if they knew, they tended to have this impression from the ‘80s and ‘90s that Chinese wine wasn’t very well made.”

On the Importance of Burying Vines in Chinese Vineyards

JW: “…In the north of China, what you have is this very cold and dry condition in the winter. So despite the fact that you might be semi-arid, you know, have really amazing, dry growing conditions in the summer, in the winter it’s so dry and so cold that the vines cannot survive the winter. So in the north of China, you have to bury the vines. You know, you have to bury after harvest around October, November, and then dig it all up again around March, April. So, you can imagine that’s very intensive work, and also it does have an impact on the health and the longevity of the vines themselves as well. Yunnan is one area where you can avoid that. But now, you know, there’s all sorts of things that’re going on in China in terms of studying varieties and learning viticulture techniques to see whether we can minimize or, in the future, eliminate the need for burying. So that’s a really unique and interesting area of study that’s also going on…”

Eddie McDougall: “The burying side, just to touch on that, there’s attempts of technology, there’s attempts of alternative methods like blankets, insulated blankets, different types of cover crop that might be able to, you know, be overgrown and put over the top. None of it has really proven to work as well as the burial… I think they’ve got more ability to mechanize the digging up of the soil first and then tipping it on top, which has improved significantly. It’s not like a guy with a shovel just tipping it over top of a vine. it’s now more mechanized. But it does, as Janet said earlier, it does impact significantly the longevity of the vines… ability to age.”

On the Chinese General Public’s Changing Relationship with Wine

EM: “No, it’s changed a lot. And I’ve seen a lot of new, what they call ‘bistros’ in, you know, the first tier cities and second tier cities across China. There’s really great wine lists everywhere. You know, there’s probably thousands and thousands and thousands of students who went through the WSET program, and that’s one of the things that really onboarded a lot of, you know, the Chinese wine consumers to embrace wine, to be more knowledgeable, to be more open about it in a global sense.

I mean, that–talk about disturbing the soil. Or, I mean, from that element, is that something that’s being discussed yet or is it just part and parcel?

EM

Yeah, look, I think it is being discussed and there are some producers who are going biodynamic and taking this sort of this sort of philosophy more seriously in their own practices and there’s a couple now who are demeter certified, right? Silver Heights being one of those, which is one of the one of the real leaders of Chinese wines who’ve gone export and done very well. You know, they they’ve gone in yeah and they’ve done really well you know, in championing that and holding true to it. It’s very tough to do it. lots and lots of investment to maintain it and of course you need to stick by the rules that they provide you. So there are attempts to do it. it’s too early yet to really understand the impact or what’s coming. but you know China’s very quick at learning and the the speed that they learn, the speed that they innovate, the speed that they create something and then fix it and then do it a thousand times better is a really short amount of time. so, you know, watch this space.

CP

Yeah. Right. Well, and I can imagine that other producers seeing Silver Heights success at a global level and farming that way is inspirational too, you know, is something that they’re going, hey, they’re doing it and they’re doing pretty well. so that knock-on effect.

EM

Mm, mm. Yeah. Yeah. Totally.

CP

So I want to talk about the economics in a few minutes of export and those things. But historically the Chinese haven’t exactly embraced their own wines. Why is that? Could you talk about a couple of reasons why? And then we’ll talk about why that is changing.

JW

So first of all, I kind of mentioned that we had a not very continuous culture of grape wine. And recently, you know, in the last let’s just say the last thirty years or so, wine because Chinese people tend to drink wine in a social context. We don’t tend to drink at home by ourselves, right? So wine for the last 30 years or so, it was really attached to this idea of social status. You know, a lot of the wine was given as gift or being seen to be consumed in a posh restaurant, you know, the sort of setting where you want to show that you’re sophisticated. And really if that’s your reason to drink wine, then quite frankly, typically people would seek out Bordeaux or Burgundy or these old world already very famous wines that would immediately impart this level of sophistication and you know that sort of thing. So Chinese people tended to for a long period wanted to drink if they’re consuming grape wine, they tend to want to drink Bordeaux, burgundies. And Bordeaux has this very handy classification system. So you know, Lafite, great, first growth. A lot of faces being given and received, right? So Chinese wine by itself didn’t quite carry that sort of cachet. And secondly, one thing we skipped was when reform and opening up started when China started to make European style wine, it wasn’t until 2004 there was something called half juice wine, was completely banned in China. So what that means was grape wine could have been made with the addition of water or fruit juice to make it sweet, diluted, you know. and that practice was allowed up to 2004. After China joined the WTO in 2001, they decided we need to bring our standard to international sort of level, so that exported wine is what people in the global market would expect. So unfortunately there were also a lot of people, if you tried Chinese wine in the eighties, nineties up to you know 2004, you probably had something not terribly pleasant, certainly not very well made.

So that’s another reason why people may have had preconceived notion that Chinese wine just wasn’t very good at all. so for those two reasons, Chinese people tended to feel that wine, good wine, top quality wine, was a foreign product. It had to come from France, Italy, Australia, even, you know. imported wine was considered higher quality than domestically produced wine. And that’s also one of the reasons why it had been quite tricky, even outside of China, to get the Chinese diaspora to really be proud of what China was producing. Most people don’t even know that China was producing wine. And secondly, if they knew they they tended to have this impression from the eighties and nineties that Chinese wine wasn’t very well made. Yeah.

EM

Yeah, also the education across, you know, the various sales channels and the distribution points. Like I remember coming to China, you know, in the nineties and you’d see stuff just sitting on a shelf, like in the sun, right? Just baking in there and you could see the cork just, you know, expanding and popping up. And it was just I mean, I don’t know how long it would have been sitting there for, but it was you know, it was must have been sitting there for a very long time for that to happen.

And at the same time the what people drank in China was mostly brandy, cognac, like VSOP. that was the celebration drink. of course it’s, you know, got a level of prestige to it. And it’s it’s it was the the hit of alcohol and the the way that you consumed it. Everything was a skull and a downing of it. didn’t really lead to much of a sophisticated wine swirl, sniff, appreciate, savour the taste experience.

And so that level of appreciation and sophistication wasn’t there. That’s voluntarily changed out. Now it’s yeah, now people geek out over the type of glass where they usually how many times they need to decant the white wine before they serve it.

it’s just another level now. Now it’s just incredible. But the education piece is massive.

CP

Well, and that’s what what brings me to my next question, which you’re basically already touching upon, which is even I noticed while I was in Macau how how many somms and just guests who were just so excited to be there and to learn about their own wines and wines from other parts of the world too. I mean, we there was some amazing seminars on Australian wine and some beautiful burgundies, but really, they were really excited about their own wines. And that seems to me to this sort of more drink local mindset, this pride, pride in homegrown wines to be a very recent thing. So, what are the factors? I mean, the education side, what what is changing to to shift, I guess, more the education of the you know, quote unquote general public and and just cultural differences of drinking wine maybe at home in a more casual setting or is it still very much a special occasion drink?

EM

No, it’s changed a lot. And I’ve seen a lot of new what they call bistros in, you know, the first tier cities and second tier cities across all China. There’s really great wine lists everywhere. you know, there’s probably thousands and thousands and thousands of students who went through the WSET program. and that’s one of the things that really onboarded a lot of you know, the Chinese wine consumers to embrace wine to be more knowledgeable, to be more open about it in a global sense. But I think the bit where it’s come full circle for me anyway, where I’ve noticed it, and again the pandemic was a trigger of this, was when a lot of the talent that was not in China that was being educated outside of China, whether it’s in winemaking or whether it’s in working at the French laundry as a similar, all went back to China, went back to see family, stayed in China as a result of pandemic and you thought why not let’s give it a crack and start making wines there or let’s open a restaurant, and let’s start exploring a bit more. And the confidence grew and I really feel that the younger generation have a lot to thank for this huge movement and huge sort of love for Chinese wines now. And I I think there’s not only obviously the patriot element, but they’ve just brought back experience and they just know what they want and you know no longer is it a question of quality or experience or knowledge or anything. It’s just a matter of time now. I think that that confidence will just continue to snowball. And the world’s embracing it. Like you see restaurants in London, Chinese restaurants in London die for Chinese wines by the glass. And that’s really happening. And Janet would have seen that firsthand, right?

CP

Yeah, I was gonna ask that was actually my next question for Janet was how are you seeing it from the UK perspective? Because the UK, you know, as you know, I lived there for a long time too. It always to me has been very much the center of wine in so many ways from the–

JW

Yeah, possibly.

CP

from the actual drinking, you know. I mean, making that’s a newer thing, but from the actual drinking perspective, and whatever Londoners are drinking is usually kind of where the rest of the world goes.

It’s a really important hub. I mean, I think New Yorkers would argue that they have a bit of a say in this too. But I would say just geographically as well, where London is the doorstep of all these European countries. So where does Chinese wine fit? Because you’ve been championing it for so long in the UK. how has I know it’s been an uphill battle at times, but are you seeing some shift in the British mindset of drinking Chinese wines?

JW

I definitely would say so, yeah. And in in no small part, thanks to what Eddie’s done with the Wynn award, because what happens now, you can say before, for example, I have to go and say, “Hey, you know, it’s nearly Chinese New Year, why do you, you know, why not try some Chinese wine?” I would have to say this to Chinese people or like organizations and wine clubs who may or may not consider it. But now, you know, people will ask me months in advance, “do you have something that I can have to surprise my friends or host the events with.” So that shift just from you know the inquiries I’m getting is one thing that has definitely changed. And then you know with what Eddie’s saying with the Wynn competition as well now, you know, the winning wines are now being carried by Cathay Pacific, for example.

you see them on the wine list of Michelin star restaurants in Hong Kong, in Singapore, in Shanghai. And people in London would notice that. You know, people in London who are hotel owners or restaurant owners or even diners, you know, there’s like, I saw Chinese wine on the wine list of cafes, lounge list or so so where can I drink this? So people are taking notice at the high end for sure that they are wanting and asking where we can start to introduce some Chinese wines to our customers. So that is a really welcoming shift. But in London you’re seeing sort of this top-down sort of filtering effect. So it starts at the top end, top restaurants are starting to ask the questions. And then gradually now we’re starting to see Chinatown restaurants, you know, the mid-tier restaurants, starting to notice, you know, if the high-end restaurants are having these wines, can we have a range that’s a bit more mid-level, but you know, maybe we’ll do a tasting menu with them for our Chinese New Year special banquet and things like that. So you’re starting, I’m starting to have these conversations now with mid-tier restaurants, which is a fantastic phenomenon because I have always felt that Chinese restaurants is the most natural carrier and the ambassador to promote Chinese wines. Because if you go to Chinese restaurants, Chinese food is already so popular. And if people, if diners have the opportunity to try wine by the glass, that for me would be the most natural way to promote Chinese wines. And we are starting to see that shift in London. I think it’s very, very exciting, very positive. Yeah.

CP

Yeah.

Great. And Eddie I mean, you’re, you know, you live in Macau, I know now, but you’re back and forth to Australia all the time. You have beautiful wines that you make under your EJ McDougall and flying winemaker labels that are so beautiful. so you know the Australian market very, very well too. So I’m curious, not only are the Australians drinking more Chinese wines, being I mean, I guess they’re closer than we are to China. Not exactly on the doorstep, but not too far away. 

And also from an export perspective, do you think that there is more education? There, the Chinese are embracing their own wines. Do you think we’re gonna therefore see more export of Chinese wines around the world? And also, what are some challenges to that? Because we touched on like burying vines, very expensive. So the final wines is there are some price barriers that they’re going to struggle with and already do struggle with. So if you could talk about that side of things, it’d be great.

EM

Yeah, there’s quite a lot to unpack on that one. You know, just speaking about Australia in general, the interest and actually not even interest anymore, the fact that it’s actually happening right now is that there are Chinese wines being sold at some of the great restaurants around Sydney and Melbourne, and even in Brisbane. And in fact I think I believe the best wine list in Australia, which was a place in Brisbane, has the most comprehensive Chinese wine list for the country. and that was crazy. I was just like, what? In Brisbane?

CP

Bris-Vegas, baby.

JW

Yeah.

EM

And so that was really, really cool to see. And that’s certainly happening. And if you know, draw a straight line north and go to places like Malaysia or Singapore, there’s a lot of Chinese people there, a lot of very proud Chinese people in those parts. And actually where some of these wines are being produced resonates with a lot of these people because that’s their original province that they’re from.

So when they see these wines, it’s particularly in places like Singapore and Malaysia, they’re like, wow, this is awesome. This is like our local wine. And they’re very happy to buy it, they’re very happy to serve it. In fact most of the people that are from China who are living in those parts of the world are incredibly wealthy. ’cause they own, you know, big factories or they own mines or they have big tech businesses or whatever it is.

So they’re drinking it and they’re proudly serving it at their own family home dinners and so forth. So it’s certainly expanding and you talk about things like the barriers to export and exporting any food product out of China is difficult. The certifications that you require, the money you need to pay, the documentation that you need to provide is never easy. Once you’ve done it a few times, you can manage it but it is difficult from that standpoint. So that’s one barrier for a lot of producers, and that’s why they see only a very select few have the export capabilities, because the investment into export markets is also not cheap. So traveling out of China for these people who you know have you know a huge market at home may not see the value of that. But the pricing of the wines has always been the big talking point over the last sort of four or five years. You know, as Janet said, it’s all been top down. It’s always gone like, let’s just go for the top, let’s charge as much as we can, build up the reputation or build up the optics of being super premium. and it works up to a certain point, and it works particularly well in China. But when you start rivaling yourself against the rest of the world’s wines, whether it’s Chile or Argentina, Spain, Italy, you know, you name it, everyone – the price matters. And you’re basically adding to the equation is like to a consumer, it’s like, you know, do they want to take the risk for that, say, $150 US dollar bottle? Or do they want to drink something that they really already know for $150 US? So it’s being addressed now. Some producers are addressing it by just, you know, making things like without oak, for example, going stainless steel for whites, or you know, choosing, you know, varieties that probably have higher yields or experimenting and looking at other regions you know, not that don’t require so much heavy lifting. But it’s gonna take some time and and it’s gonna take a lot more scale and probably with China a lot more automation. I mean I was at the OIV General Assembly in Ningxia and there was a presentation on all this new vineyard technology that was being applied in China. I mean if they apply half of what I saw, they’re not gonna need a single human to walk in the vineyard for the next twelve months. It’ll be all done. It’ll be on the boat. All by robots.

CP

Yeah, I mean that’s another existential conversation for another time.

EM

Totally.

JW

Yeah.

EM

But that’s happening and so that like when that comes to all reducing those costs and and bringing the end unit price down for an export market, they can eventually become more competitive. But I still feel there’s a bit of time in that. it’s not gonna happen.

CP

And as I was emailing with you guys, I saw about the OIV, the World Congress of Vine and Wine. It was their first time ever in Asia, right? That was just a few weeks ago. I figured you were probably there.

EM

Yeah. Yeah.

CP

Which I thought was, you know, all just an interesting statement and testament to the seriousness of Chinese wine, really on a global scale. Yeah, I kinda, I don’t know that we should go there with the automation. Cause I think that’s also a little scary, for all of us globally speaking. But you know, certainly some positives, some negatives, a lot to be scared about, a lot to be hopeful about. And I think we’ll leave it there because I think you have given us so much amazing information. And I think it’s really super exciting to see where China, Chinese wine, how far it has come, as you say, in such an extraordinarily short period of time, the modern Chinese wine world, and also how much we have to be excited about for the future.

And I think you know, it is tough to get Chinese wine here. We have a lot of geopolitical reasons for that. But we have given some coverage on Wine Enthusiast to some fantastic Chinese wines that are getting over here and being poured in some of the same kind of those trendy New York bars and restaurants that you touched upon. So it isn’t entirely impossible. and we certainly would like to see more of it. But I would give another shout out to Janet’s amazing book, The Chinese Wine Renaissance, because I think if you wanna just a really fantastic overview of I mean, you wrote it in 2019, it still feels really relevant. I’m sure there’s things you would add to it today, right? In the last seven years. 

JW

Yeah. There was a reprint in 2024.

EM

There’s an update, isn’t it? There’s an update.

JW

Yeah, there was an update in 24. Yeah.

CP

Yeah, that’s right, that’s right.

JW

So hopefully the one you have is the slightly updated one. But yes, I did write it with the intention so that it doesn’t date. So I covered a lot of cultural history, background to explain why it’s even happening. And the hope is that it’s something that doesn’t date too quickly because like you say, Eddie, you know, things happen so fast in China, you know, the the ink wouldn’t be dry before it’s already outdated if you want to really keep up with the latest of developments.

CP

But it’s a fantastic overview, you know, for folks like me who even with twenty years in the wine industry is really coming to this like brand new. So this for me is a real, it gave me a fantastic overview, and I think other folks too. So I really recommend that. Go out and find Eddie’s wines. Eddie, your wines aren’t here in the States, your EJ McDougall wines?

EM

No, we had a bit of a false start with some people on the east coast. I think it was something to do with some tariffs or something that were being put onto wines.

CP

You know, we got the whole episode without saying the T word, Eddie.

EM

So, so unfortunately not. I think it sort of made a lot of importers and distributors, you know, quite adverse to any sort of new risk, you know, and they just wanted to play it very safe ’cause they weren’t sure whether or not they’d have a portfolio the next day or not, or if they’d be, you know, doubling down on it. So yeah, not yet, but we are actively looking and actively you know, getting ourselves out there and yeah, we don’t produce a lot, but you know, we certainly would love to be in the US at some point.

CP

And they’re gorgeous wines, you have no problem. I think I imagine you’re probably allocating at this point. They’re pretty beautiful wines that a lot of people want to drink. And so congrats on that in general, because I think you’re just a very… it’s going full guns. I keep hearing lots of buzz about it and having tried the wines, I completely understand why. So thank you both for your time. I really appreciate it. And until next time, till we meet again in Macau.

Letter from the Publisher

Risky Business

Preserving a family legacy requires the courage to change it.

When we think about family businesses and strategy, it often comes back to risk aversion. This philosophy is consistent across nearly all privately held family companies. Of course, there are exceptions, but time and time again, I hear it repeated as a core tenet of company culture. With an estimated 95% of wineries being family-owned or -operated, it’s essentially an industry-wide philosophy.

Read More

As a second-generation business leader, I am constantly in a delicate dance of maintaining a company’s legacy while taking risks for growth. And yet, as we experience a barrage of changes in wine culture and agriculture, we’re seeing these pressures force the next generation to think very differently than any generation before.

Bordeaux just had its hottest growing season on record. Champagne had to temporarily raise its alcohol requirements for the first time. They’re ripping out Zinfandel vines in California and selling out of Sancerre at your local shop. I can tell you that each and every one of these families will be sitting around this holiday season discussing—or, more likely, handwringing and debating—these pressures and how to deal with them.

So what is the solution when tradition, legacy, and conservation are the pillars of your business playbook?

Throw the playbook away.

Not because it’s not important or valuable, but because what got you here will no longer get you where you need to go. That sounds scary, but it can also be very exciting. The pressure and burden of it all could either crack or inspire.

This year’s Family Issue highlights the brilliance of wine families and the sheer forces of change being thrust upon them. For what is a crisis if not an opportunity for ruthless creativity? Being brave and embracing radical change is now a path born of necessity.

We’re at an incredibly important moment of evolution. And if we’re lucky, the next generation will inherit a legacy not just of tradition, but of bravery and resilience.

title: The Italian Wine Renaissance Is Happening Right Now
summary:
At Vinitaly.USA, some 300 exhibitors presented 2,500 wines, offering an expansive look at Italy's extraordinary diversity.

The post The Italian Wine Renaissance Is Happening Right Now appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
For an industry that has spent much of the past year discussing its challenges, Italian wine arrived in New York City with a different message: There’s plenty to be excited about. 

Held October 26 to 27 at Pier 36, Vinitaly.USA welcomed more than 3,000 wine professionals from 40 countries and 20 U.S. states, a 36% increase over last year’s Chicago edition. Some 300 exhibitors presented 2,500 wines, offering an expansive look at Italy’s extraordinary diversity.

The mood was upbeat and the energy palpable—there was no mistaking that Italy was excited to be in New York. Producers, buyers, sommeliers, and journalists filled the aisles, tasting, talking, and making connections. Across regions and styles, quality was a recurring theme. 

Historic appellations demonstrated their vitality, while lesser-known varieties and regions offered exciting discoveries. Sparkling wine made from Pecorino (the grape) in the Marche surprised even the most jaded of wine professionals.

“The curiosity at the Wine Enthusiast Bubble Lounge was wonderful to see,” says Wine Enthusiast Tasting Director Anna-Christina Cabrales. “Jeff Porter’s selections had people asking questions, comparing notes, and coming back for another pour. We were busy from start to finish! It showed the excitement for Italian sparkling wine, as its range is so broad and guests were eager to explore all of it.”

Across the board, contemporary label designs reflected a willingness to rethink how Italian wine presents itself to the world.  Similarly, the younger generation of winemakers brought a confidence that was hard to miss. They know the history of their estates, and they’re proud of it. But they’re not interested in standing still. Whether experimenting with new styles, rethinking packaging, or finding new ways to reach consumers, they’re making it clear that the next chapter of Italian wine will have their fingerprints all over it.

For Steven McDonald, Master Sommelier and Executive Wine Director at Pappas Bros. Steakhouse, the event was as much about building relationships as discovering wines. 

“Vinitaly USA was a great opportunity to connect with established importers and wineries and also meet new wineries looking for representation,” McDonald said. “It was exciting to get to speak about the market in Texas and suggest some strategies to help wineries and importers to take advantage of its potential.”

Education also took center stage, with seminars ranging from “The Future of Wine Tourism” to “Metodo Classico Today.” More than 1,690 business meetings took place, while the wine2wine Vinitaly Business Forum explored shifting consumer habits and market opportunities. But Italian wine has always been about more than business.

“Vinitaly NYC was a reminder of how much Italian wine has to say beyond what’s in the glass,” said Jessica Dupuy, journalist and author of Italianity: The Culture of Italian Wine. “There’s a real opportunity to bring more of that spirit to American consumers: give people a story they connect with and an experience that makes them feel welcome.”

title: Family Dinners Are a Lost Art. Bringing Them Back Could Save Our Humanity
summary:
It doesn’t matter what’s on the table, as long as you’re gathered around it together.

The post Family Dinners Are a Lost Art. Bringing Them Back Could Save Our Humanity appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
It has taken me nearly 45 years to realize that food and drink are the primary sources of my family’s greatest conflicts—and also our greatest connections.

My first inkling came when my husband, an introvert to my extrovert, hid himself in my childhood bedroom during his first Christmas with my Italian-American family. We were yell-talking about the meal, the wines, and the table setting in what I thought was a perfectly normal manner. To him, World War III had broken out. Growing up in Australia in a split-family home, he had meat-potato-veg meals mostly cooked in a microwave—eaten without fuss or fanfare, and definitely without yell-talking. Food was a means to an end.

My family, on the other hand, thought about, argued about, prepped, and eventually cooked food pretty much from the time we woke up. At first, the food itself was fairly simple. The 1980s and ’90s were an especially dire time for food culture in middle-class America. Lunchables were ubiquitous, and everything was “fat-free.” Still, while the meals were straightforward, the sense of ceremony was not. Each night, my parents, my sibling, and I gathered around the table. A Spyro Gyra record (later, a cassette tape) played elevator jazz through the enormous speakers in the living room, my mother with a glass of high-octane, butterscotchy Chardonnay, my father with a low-end California Zinfandel.

Our nightly communion was hardly serene. Many of my dinner-table memories involve my parents pleading with my sibling and me to eat another bite of limp, cold asparagus, and reprimanding us for belting out bawdy songs about farts. But I also remember the silly “in-family” jokes, anecdotes my parents would share from their childhood, or ones we’d recount from that day at school.

By the early 2000s, once my sibling and I had ventured off to college, the family meals we shared when we reunited became even more momentous, though not necessarily more tranquil, a somewhat foreign concept to a pack of passionate, opinionated personalities like ours.

Eventually, my husband warmed up to our family mealtimes. These days, he no longer hides in the bedroom. As parents ourselves, we have found dinnertime in our own home to be as precious and chaotic as it was when I was growing up. We bribe, beg, and barter with our young daughters to eat their vegetables, bark at them for the millionth time to stop leaning back in their chairs, and to chew with their mouths closed. We also laugh a lot and play card games, “Simon Says,” or “Telephone” while I sip English bubbles or a dirty martini and my husband unwinds with a cold beer or an Old Fashioned.

On some of the tougher days, when my kids have poured half a bottle of ketchup over my perfectly seasoned roast chicken and spilled the rest on the carpet, I wonder whether it’s worth sticking with this dinnertime routine.

And then I remember that family meals serve as an antidote to the glowing, incessantly noisy electronic rectangle so often glued to my hand. They are the moments when I am most present with my family, creating memories that will linger longer than anything on that screen. In the cracks between the chaos of family mealtime is where love grows. It’s where our humanity lies. I wouldn’t trade it for the world.
